taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes it was long treated as conspecific with Mallard (AOU 1983, 1998) and was newly separated as a species by AOS (2020) based on assortative mating and genomic data.
fieldMarks: Both sexes resemble a female Mallard with mottled brown plumage but somewhat darker overall, especially on the tail and undertail
Blue wing patch (speculum) with white borders that may be narrower than a Mallard's
Male bill bright yellow; female's dull olive to orange
behavior: Not truly migratory; seasonal local movements, gathering at permanent lakes and rivers in dry seasons and spreading out in rainy seasons
Forages in water by dabbling, head-and-neck submerging or up-ending, rarely diving; also grazes and grubs on land
Mostly plant material (seeds, stems, roots, waste grain), also insects, crustaceans, mollusks and tadpoles
Male gives a thin rreeb; female quacks loudly
habitat: Mostly shallow freshwater marshes of lakes and ponds, slow lowland rivers and irrigated farmland.
range: Breeds from southeastern Arizona, southern New Mexico and west-central Texas south into the Mexican highlands. Non-breeding birds occur casually north through much of Colorado and Utah; accidental in California, Wyoming and Nebraska.

lookalikes.name: Mallard (female)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mexican Duck is somewhat darker, especially on the tail and undertail, with narrower white wing-patch borders.

lookalikes.name: Mottled duck
lookalikes.howToTell: NatureServe notes difficulty separating Mexican Duck from Mottled Duck may be reducing detection of one or both.
